query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A small tungsten addition to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA will enhance its high-temperature stability and resistance to creep and corrosion, while preserving its ductile behavior for use in fasteners under extreme service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine, uniform lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor amount (e.g., 2–5 atomic %) of tungsten into the alloy composition, partially replacing one or more of the base elements.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant environments including extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep conditions, and corrosive environments similar to those encountered in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners.
generation.structural_mediator: Tungsten atoms are expected to segregate at phase boundaries and grain interfaces, thereby pinning the lamellar structure and refining local microstructures.
generation.mechanism: The presence of tungsten is predicted to slow down dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding (thereby reducing creep) by acting as obstacles to defect migration. In addition, tungsten may promote the formation of more stable, protective oxide scales that improve the alloy's passivation behavior and resistance to corrosion. Its limited addition is aimed at enhancing high-temperature properties without introducing brittle phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the base AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, the tungsten-modified alloy should exhibit a lower creep rate under long-term loading, improved stability and integrity of the passive film in corrosive environments, and similar levels of ductility and strength under ambient conditions.
generation.baseline: The current performance metrics of the conventional AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, which already provides a good strength–ductility combination but exhibits limitations in long-term creep and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated only with low tungsten contents; excessive tungsten may lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds. The benefits are expected within typical service temperature ranges and corrosive conditions relevant to fastener applications and may not extrapolate to extremely high-temperature or aggressive environments outside the tested range.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal tungsten concentration and its long-term effects on ductility and microstructural stability require further investigation, as excessive additions could compromise toughness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy batches: one of the standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and one modified with a selected tungsten content (e.g., ~3 at.% W). Process both alloys under identical casting and heat-treatment conditions to ensure comparable lamellar microstructures. Subject specimens from each batch to long-term creep tests (e.g., under constant load at room temperature and at moderately elevated temperatures such as 700°C) as well as accelerated corrosion tests in a chloride-containing acid solution simulating service environments.
measurements: Record creep strain versus time to determine creep rate under identical loading conditions
Perform electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization to assess passive film stability and corrosion current densities
Conduct tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate and an improved passive film stability (or lower corrosion current density) compared to the baseline, or if the modification leads to a marked decrease in ductility or unexpected brittle behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD (calculation of phase diagrams) method can also provide an insightful guidance to design EHEAs, on the premise that reliable thermodynamics database for HEAs are to be established and completed. In summary, here we proposed a novel strategy to design high-entropy alloys (HEAs), i.e., the concept of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), to solve the challenging issues for this new type of advanced metallic materials, including the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility, and the inferior castability and compositional segregation. Based on the new strategy, we successfully designed a highly uniform AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, with an unprecedented combination of castability, high fracture strength and high ductility. The bulk EHEA ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared by the conventional casting method using the commercially pure raw materials. The EHEA exhibited a fine lamellar microstructure consisting of coupled grown fcc/B2 phases. Our design strategy is of great significance in both scientific and technical aspects, and can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs.
